content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit is a light baked product made from eggs, sugar, flour and a small amount of fat. The batter is whisked into an airy foam and then baked at a low temperature, giving the biscuit a porous structure and a gentle flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Biscuit originated in Europe in the 19th century as a yeast‑free light cake.
Traditional biscuit is often used as a base for layered cakes because it absorbs syrups well.
In Russia, “biscuit layers” are a popular component of multi‑layered desserts.
Biscuit can be made sweet or slightly savory depending on added ingredients.
Sometimes starch replaces part of the wheat flour to achieve an even lighter texture.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Biscuit usually contains only a small amount of butter, making it less caloric than many other baked goods.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Biscuit provides a quick source of energy thanks to its carbohydrate content.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the recipe add a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The porous crumb aids digestion, especially in light‑diet regimes.

items.title: Fortification potential
items.content: Vitamins, minerals or protein powders can be incorporated into the batter, making the biscuit more nutritious.

items.title: Egg or gluten allergy
items.content: Biscuit contains eggs and wheat, which may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of its sugar and simple carbohydrate content, biscuit can raise blood glucose quickly.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and dental caries.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Biscuit loses freshness rapidly and can become dry or moldy if not stored properly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Biscuit is used as a cake base, in dessert parfaits, or as a light snack on its own. It can be soaked with fruit or cream syrups, topped with frosting, jam, or fresh berries. For a more nutritious version, add nuts, dried fruit, or protein powder to the batter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep biscuit in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2–3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 1 week) or freeze (up to 2 months). Allow it to reach room temperature before serving to retain its soft texture.
